title: Highly uniform first-electron position in qubit arrays fabricated on dedicated QSOI(R) 300mm commercial platform
authors: Johan Pelloux-Prayer, Elise Prin, Giselle A. Elbaz, Pierre-Louis Julliard, Amaryllis Comiti, Clément Nguyen, Sylvain Martin, Patrick Torresani, Renan Lethiecq, Carlos Augusto Suarez Segovia, Franck Arnaud, Etienne Nowak, Tristan Meunier, Bruna Cardoso Paz
abstract: We report progress toward the development of a quantum silicon-on-insulator (QSOI(R)) technology compatible with 300mm CMOS fabrication and adapted from the 28nm Fully-Depleted SOI (28nm FD-SOI) platform for scalable quantum computing. We compare quantum devices fabricated with standard 28nm FD-SOI and QSOI(R) technologies, and show striking improvements of room temperature electrostatic properties of the individual device. Moreover, the QSOI(R) technology has significantly reduced the device variability and the dispersion of device properties at the wafer level. Transistor metrics are reproduced by TCAD simulations showing that the electrostatics of the devices behave as expected for QSOI(R) technology. Wafer-scale measurements at sub-2K show reproducible quantum dots down to the few-electron regime with 69\% yield for successful charge detection of the first electron and a dispersion of the first electron position of $\mathrm{\pm 35 mV}$ over 377 quantum dots. These results establish QSOI(R) as a promising platform for CMOS-compatible quantum device co-integration.
summary: This paper reports on the development of a Quantum Silicon-on-Insulator (QSOI(R)) platform, showing it is compatible with 300mm CMOS fabrication for quantum computing. By comparing it to older technologies, the authors demonstrate significant improvements in device uniformity and low variability in quantum dot charge detection. These results establish QSOI(R) as a promising, scalable foundation for integrated quantum devices.
main_problem: The primary goal is to develop a scalable, highly uniform, and CMOS-compatible platform for fabricating qubit arrays.
main_result: The QSOI(R) technology significantly improves device uniformity and reduces variability compared to standard FD-SOI, demonstrating reproducible quantum dot operation down to the few-electron regime on a wafer scale.
method: The research involves comparative electrical characterization of quantum devices fabricated using QSOI(R) versus 28nm FD-SOI, utilizing both room-temperature and cryogenic measurements.
model_or_system: The system is a quantum dot array fabricated on a Quantum Silicon-on-Insulator (QSOI(R)) platform, adapted from 28nm FD-SOI, designed for integrating silicon spin qubits.
key_observables: First electron position dispersion ($\pm 35	ext{mV}$), threshold voltage ($	ext{V}_{	ext{TH}}$) distribution ($\sigma	ext{V}_{	ext{TH}}$), subthreshold swing (SS), and charge detection yield ($	ext{69\%}$).
important_parameters: Operating temperatures ($	ext{300K}$ and $	ext{sub-2K}$), device dimensions (28nm), and uniformity metrics.
main_assumptions: The electrostatics of the devices are assumed to behave as predicted by TCAD simulations, and the platform is assumed to be compatible with 300mm CMOS fabrication.

paper_structure: The paper progresses by first establishing the need for scalable platforms, then presenting comparative electrical measurements (room and cryogenic) showing superior uniformity and performance of QSOI(R) over existing technologies, and concluding with the demonstration of wafer-scale quantum dot functionality.
why_interesting: The demonstration of high uniformity and low variability in charge detection parameters at the wafer scale is crucial for scaling up any solid-state quantum computing architecture, providing a tangible engineering milestone.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Schematic of an array of quantum dots using QSOI®. Access gates (AG) are used to form electrostatic reservoirs. Plungers gates (G1, G2,..., Gx) are used to control the chemical potential of the quantum dots. Barriers (B1, B2, ..., Bx+1) are repurposed vias used to control the tunnel coupling between two neighboring quantum dots. This is an artist impression and does not reflect the real dimensions of our devices.

Data are colored in blue for 28nm FD-SOI and in pink for QSOI® in a, b, c, and d. a) Wafer-level Id-Vg across the center, mid and edge radii (28 dies). b) - c) Boxplot of the threshold voltage for 28nm FD-SOI and QSOI® against the applied back-gate voltage in (b) and the barrier-vias voltage in (c). Box plots show the interquartile range and the median. Whiskers represent the maximum and minimum values without outliers. Outliers are defined as data points that are more than 1.5 interquartile range away from the median. d) Boxplot of the subthreshold swing (StS) extracted from Id-Vg curve for 3 back gate biases: 0V, 1V, and 2V. Fig. 3. Simulation and experimental data obtained for a linear array with 3 plunger gates in series. Left: transfer characteristics at room temperature for different back-gate bias VBG = 0, 1, and 2V, and VDS = 50mV. Right: Extracted threshold voltage as a function of the back-gate voltage at room and low temperatures.

Fig. 4. Left: Schematics of a charge detection configuration on a bilinear device, where a single-electron transistor is used to sense the electrons tunneling inside the quantum dot. Right: Stability diagram showing the few- electron regime for the probed quantum dot formed underneath the plunger gate. The numbers inside the figure indicate the charge occupation of the probed QD. The interruption of the regular pattern of vertical jumps indicates that the dot has been emptied. Access gates are not shown for simplicity.

Fig. 5. Left: Wafermap of charge detection at the wafer scale for a pair of facing plunger gates. Only 4 dies were not measured since our protocol to find the first Coulomb peak rejected these dies. Each die shows the measurement between plunger gates G3T and G3B. Right: Histogram of the first electron position across the wafer measured for all the possible detectors in our device.
